transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Hearing loss genetics, for Friday, November 27.
Let's turn to hearing loss genetics, where we have one new preprint today.
It's from the Alsina lab, posted on bioRxiv. The question is what sall1a does in the inner ear. It's the zebrafish counterpart of SALL1, the gene behind Townes-Brocks syndrome.
They first looked at timing. In hair cells, sall1a turns on after Pou4f3 and Gfi1, two well-known factors in hair-cell development. So it acts downstream of the early specification program.
That fits with what they found when they knocked it out with CRISPR. Hair cells are still specified, but they don't mature properly.
The mutants have fewer active hair cells and lose expression of mature hair-cell genes. At the whole-animal level they show balance defects and a weaker startle response.

So the defect shows up at the cellular, molecular and behavioral levels, which makes the maturation story more convincing. It also suggests a possible mechanism for the inner-ear side of Townes-Brocks syndrome.
A few cautions, though. This is a preprint and hasn't been peer reviewed, and we only have the summary to go on, so we can't say anything about effect sizes or how many fish they studied.
It's also a zebrafish model. Zebrafish hair cells are a powerful system, but whether mammalian SALL1 plays the same maturation role still needs to be tested directly.
The takeaway: sall1a seems to act after hair cells are specified, as a switch for their maturation, which gives Townes-Brocks hearing loss a plausible developmental explanation to test in mammals.

papers.title: Sall1a, a transcription factor responsible for the Townes-Brocks syndrome, is involved in hair cell maturation
